content.content:
1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
64

11	
12	\chapter{Overview}
13	\chaplabel{overview}
14	
15	\note{Keyword and varargs parameters,
16	array comprehensions,
17	dimensions and units,
18	tests and properties,
19	distributions,
20	some ASCII conversion, and
21	some common types are not yet supported.
22	
23	Some examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter.}
24	
25	In this chapter, we provide a high-level overview of the entire Fortress
26	language. We present most features in this chapter through the use of examples,
27	which should be accessible to programmers of other languages.
28	In this chapter, unlike the rest of the specification,
29	no attempt is made to provide complete descriptions
30	of the various language features presented. Instead, we intend this overview to
31	provide useful context for reading other sections of this specification,
32	which provide rigorous definitions for what is merely
33	introduced here.
34	
35	\section{The Fortress Programming Environment}
36	\seclabel{programming-env}
37	
38	\revision{revival-environment}{\secref{programming-env} to \secref{apitool}
39	are rewritten to describe the implementation in the revival's repository.
40	Every command is printed as it runs there, with the output that it gave.
41	The Working Draft's text of these sections, which describes a store of
42	components that was not built, is kept in \secref{revival-environment}.}
43	
44	This section and the two after it show how to build the Fortress
45	implementation in the revival's repository
46	(\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}) and how to run a program with it.
47	Each command is printed as it is typed into a shell.
48	The files of the examples are printed as they are typed, in ASCII;
49	the section on rendering below shows how such code is rendered.
50	
51	A Fortress program is a \emph{component}, stored in a source file.
52	The following component is the program of this section:
53	
54	\begin{verbatim}
55	component HelloWorld
56	export Executable
57	
58	run(): () = println "Hello, world!"
59	
60	end
61	\end{verbatim}
62	
63	The first line names the component.
64	The second line is an \emph{export statement}, which \secref{overview:apis}
65	explains.
66	The fourth line defines a function \VAR{run}, which takes no parameter,
67	returns no value, and prints one line.
68	A program starts with a call of its function \VAR{run}.
69	
70	A source file must contain exactly one component declaration, and its name
71	must match the file name without the file extension \shellcommand{.fss}.
72	So this component is stored in a file named \shellcommand{HelloWorld.fss}.
73	If the two names differ, the implementation refuses the file with this
74	message:
75	
76	\begin{verbatim}
77	Component/API names must match their enclosing file names.
78	\end{verbatim}
79	
80	A program is run in one of two ways: under the interpreter, or compiled.

82	\subsection{Building the Implementation}
83	
84	The implementation needs a Java Development Kit of version 25 and Apache Ant.
85	The following commands are issued in the root folder of a checkout of the
86	repository.
87	The first line names the folder of the Java Development Kit, here the one of a
88	Debian or Ubuntu system.
89	The last line builds the implementation, in about a minute.
90	
91	\begin{verbatim}
92	export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
93	export FORTRESS_HOME=$(pwd)
94	export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$FORTRESS_HOME/bin:$PATH
95	ant compileAll
96	\end{verbatim}
97	
98	The build prints its steps.
99	Its last lines are these, with the time that the build took:
100	
101	\begin{verbatim}
102	BUILD SUCCESSFUL
103	Total time: 50 seconds
104	\end{verbatim}
105	
106	The command \shellcommand{fortress} is now on the shell's path.
107	The programs of this chapter are written in a folder of their own:
108	
109	\begin{verbatim}
110	mkdir ~/hello
111	cd ~/hello
112	\end{verbatim}
113	
114	The component above is written to the file \shellcommand{HelloWorld.fss} in
115	this folder.

117	\subsection{Running a Program under the Interpreter}
118	
119	The interpreter reads a source file and runs it:
120	
121	\begin{verbatim}
122	fortress HelloWorld.fss
123	\end{verbatim}
124	
125	The command prints:
126	
127	\begin{verbatim}
128	Hello, world!
129	\end{verbatim}
130	
131	The command \shellcommand{fortress walk HelloWorld.fss} is the same command.
132	The interpreter does not check the static types of a program.
133	A type error stops the program when the run reaches it.
134	
135	\subsection{Compiling and Running a Program}
136	
137	The compiler checks the static types of a component and writes bytecode of
138	the Java Virtual Machine for it.
139	A compiled program uses a library that is compiled first.
140	The following five commands compile it.
141	They are issued once after each build of the implementation, in the folder
142	\shellcommand{ProjectFortress} of the checkout.
143	They print nothing, and together they take about two minutes.
144	
145	\begin{verbatim}
146	cd $FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress
147	fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
148	fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
149	fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
150	fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
151	fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
152	cd ~/hello
153	\end{verbatim}
154	
155	The program is then compiled and run with two commands:
156	
157	\begin{verbatim}
158	fortress compile HelloWorld.fss
159	fortress run HelloWorld
160	\end{verbatim}
161	
162	The first command prints nothing.
163	The second prints:
164	
165	\begin{verbatim}
166	Hello, world!
167	\end{verbatim}
168	
169	The command \shellcommand{fortress compile} takes a source file.
170	It prints nothing when it succeeds, and a static error stops it with a message.
171	The command \shellcommand{fortress run} takes the name of a component, not a
172	file.
173	It runs the bytecode that the last compilation of that component wrote, and
174	compiles nothing.
175	After a change of a source file, the interpreter runs the changed program, and
176	\shellcommand{fortress run} runs the old one until the file is compiled again.
177	
178	\subsection{The Caches}
179	
180	The implementation keeps its results in \emph{caches}, so that a later command
181	can use them again.
182	The caches are folders under \shellcommand{default\_repository/caches} in the
183	checkout.
184	The folder \shellcommand{bytecode\_cache} holds one file of bytecode for each
185	compiled component, as \shellcommand{HelloWorld.jar}.
186	The folders \shellcommand{interpreter\_parsed\_cache} and
187	\shellcommand{interpreter\_cache} hold the interpreter's parsed form of each
188	file that it read, and \shellcommand{analyzed\_cache} holds the results of the
189	compiler's analysis.
190	A build that changed the implementation empties the caches, and the five
191	commands above are then issued again.

194	\section{Exports and Imports}
195	\seclabel{overview:apis}
196	
197	When a component is defined, it can include \emph{export statements}.
198	For example, the component \TYP{HelloWorld} includes the export statement
199	``\EXP{\KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}}''.
200	Export statements list various \emph{APIs}
201	that a component implements.
202	Unlike in other languages, APIs in
203	Fortress are themselves program constructs; programmers can rely on
204	standard APIs, and declare new ones. API declarations are sequences of
205	declarations of
206	variables, functions, and other program constructs, along with their
207	types and other
208	supporting declarations. For example, here is the definition of API
209	\TYP{Executable}, which the library provides:
210	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Executable.tex}
211	
212	This API contains the declaration of a single function \VAR{run},
213	which takes no argument.
214	The return type of \VAR{run} is \EXP{()}, pronounced ``void''.
215	Type \EXP{()} may be used in Fortress as a return type
216	for functions that have no meaningful return value.
217	There is a single value with type \EXP{()}:
218	the value \EXP{()}, also pronounced ``void''.
219	References to value \EXP{()} as opposed
220	to type \EXP{()} are resolved by context.
221	
222	A component that exports an API must provide a definition
223	for every program construct declared in the API.
224	For example, because the component \TYP{HelloWorld} exports the API
225	\TYP{Executable}, it must include a definition for the function \VAR{run}.
226	The compiler checks this.
227	The interpreter does not.
228	
229	An API is defined in a file with the file extension \shellcommand{.fsi}.
230	As a component's file, the file holds exactly one API, and the name of the API
231	must match the file name without the file extension.
232	For example, the following API is written to a file named
233	\shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi}:
234	
235	\begin{verbatim}
236	api Zeepf
237	
238	foo(s: String): ()
239	baz(s: String): String
240	
241	end
242	\end{verbatim}
243	
244	The following component implements this API.
245	The implementation finds the component that implements an API only under the
246	name of the API, so the component is named \TYP{Zeepf} too, and is written to
247	a file named \shellcommand{Zeepf.fss}.
248	Components and APIs exist in separate namespaces, and therefore
249	it is allowed for a component to have the same name as an API.
250	
251	\begin{verbatim}
252	component Zeepf
253	export Zeepf
254	
255	foo(s: String): () = println("foo says: " || s)
256	baz(s: String): String = s || "!"
257	
258	end
259	\end{verbatim}
260	
261	Components are also allowed to \emph{import} APIs. A component that
262	imports an API is allowed to use any of the program constructs
263	declared in that API. For example, the following component, written to a file
264	named \shellcommand{Blargh.fss}, imports the API
265	\TYP{Zeepf} and calls the functions \VAR{foo} and \VAR{baz} declared in
266	\TYP{Zeepf}:
267	
268	\begin{verbatim}
269	component Blargh
270	import Zeepf.{ foo, baz }
271	export Executable
272	
273	run(): () = foo(baz("whatever"))
274	
275	end
276	\end{verbatim}
277	
278	In an import statement of the form:
279	%import A.{S}
280	\begin{Fortress}
281	\(\KWD{import}\:A.\{S\}\)
282	\end{Fortress}
283	all names in the list of names \VAR{S} are imported from API $A$, and can be
284	referred to as unqualified names within the importing component.
285	
286	Note that no component refers directly to another component,
287	or to constructs defined in another component.
288	Instead, \emph{all external references go through APIs}.
289	This level of indirection provides a way to hide implementation details in a
290	component.
291	
292	The interpreter runs the component \TYP{Blargh} as it runs any program.
293	It finds the files of the API \TYP{Zeepf} and of the component \TYP{Zeepf} in
294	the same folder:
295	
296	\begin{verbatim}
297	fortress Blargh.fss
298	\end{verbatim}
299	
300	The command prints:
301	
302	\begin{verbatim}
303	foo says: whatever!
304	\end{verbatim}
305	
306	To run the compiled program, the component is \emph{linked}.
307	The command \shellcommand{fortress link} compiles a component and the
308	components that implement the APIs that it imports, and joins them.
309	It prints nothing when it succeeds.
310	
311	\begin{verbatim}
312	fortress link Blargh.fss
313	fortress run Blargh
314	\end{verbatim}
315	
316	The second command prints:
317	
318	\begin{verbatim}
319	foo says: whatever!
320	\end{verbatim}
321

323	\seclabel{apitool}
324	
325	The command \shellcommand{fortress api} generates an API from a component:
326	
327	\begin{verbatim}
328	fortress api Zeepf.fss
329	\end{verbatim}
330	
331	The command prints the API:
332	
333	\begin{verbatim}
334	api Zeepf
335	
336	foo(s: String): ()
337	
338	baz(s: String): String
339	
340	end
341	\end{verbatim}
342	
343	The API has the name of the component.
344	It declares every top-level definition of the component that does not include
345	the modifier \KWD{private}.
346	
347	With the option \shellcommand{-out}, the command writes the API to a file:
348	
349	\begin{verbatim}
350	fortress api -out Zeepf.fsi Zeepf.fss
351	\end{verbatim}

354

478	\subsection{Juxtaposition and function application}
479	
480	In the definition of \VAR{factorial},
481	note the juxtaposition of parameter \VAR{n} with the recursive
482	call \EXP{\VAR{factorial}(n - 1)}.
483	In Fortress, as in mathematics,
484	multiplication is represented through juxtaposition.
485	By default,
486	two expressions of numeric type that are juxtaposed
487	represent a multiplication.
488	On the other hand,
489	juxtaposition of an expression of function type
490	with another expression to its right
491	represents function application,
492	as in the following example:
493	
494	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.sin.tex}
495	
496	Moreover, juxtaposition of expressions of string type
497	represents concatenation, as in the following example:
498	
499	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.String.tex}
500	
501	In fact, juxtaposition is an operator in Fortress,
502	just like \EXP{+} and \EXP{-},
503	that is overloaded based on the runtime types of its arguments.
504	
505	There is a special case concerning juxtaposition that is important to mention:
506	When writing a numeric literal, the \emph{digit-group separator},
507	\txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE} (U+202F),
508	may be included between the digits in order to improve readability.
509	In ASCII,
510	this character can be abbreviated in the context of a numeric literal
511	(\emph{and only in this context}) with the character \txt{'}.
512	For example, the number 299,792,458 can be denoted in ASCII by the
513	following numeric literal:
514	
515	\begin{verbatim}
516	299'792'458
517	\end{verbatim}
518	
519	This literal is converted into Unicode by replacing all occurrences of
520	\txt{'} with \txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE}:
521	%299 792 458
522	\begin{Fortress}
523	\(299{}\;792{}\;458\)
524	\end{Fortress}
525	This is not an application of the juxtaposition operator;
526	rather, it is a single token.
527	Note that commas cannot be used to separate digits because ambiguities
528	would arise with the use of commas in other expressions,
529	such as tuples.
530	
531	\subsection{Keyword Parameters}
532	
533	Functions in Fortress can be defined to take keyword arguments by
534	providing default values for parameters. In
535	the following example:
536	
537	%makeColor(red:ZZ64 = 0, green:ZZ64 = 0, blue:ZZ64 = 0) =
538	%   if 0 <= red <= 255 AND 0 <= green <= 255 AND 0 <= blue <= 255
539	%   then Color(red,green,blue)
540	%   else throw Error end
541	\begin{Fortress}
542	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{red}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{green}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{blue}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0) =\)\\
543	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{if} 0 \leq \VAR{red} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{green} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{blue} \leq 255 \)\\
544	\(   \KWD{then} \TYP{Color}(\VAR{red},\VAR{green},\VAR{blue})\)\\
545	\(   \KWD{else}\;\;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error} \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
546	\end{Fortress}
547	
548	the function \VAR{makeColor} takes three keyword arguments, all of
549	which default to \EXP{0}. If we call it as follows:
550	
551	%makeColor(green = 255)
552	\begin{Fortress}
553	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{green} = 255)\)
554	\end{Fortress}
555	
556	the arguments \VAR{red} and \VAR{blue} are both given the value \EXP{0}.
557	
558	There are some other aspects of this example worth mentioning.
559	For example,
560	the body of this function consists of an \KWD{if} expression.
561	The test of the \KWD{if} expression checks that
562	all three parameters have values between \EXP{0} and \EXP{255}. The
563	boolean operator \EXP{\leq} is \emph{chained}: An expression of
564	the form \EXP{x \leq y \leq z} is equivalent to the expression
565	\EXP{x \leq y \wedge y \leq z}, just as in mathematical notation.
566	The \KWD{then} clause provides an example of a constructor call in Fortress,
567	and the \KWD{else} clause shows us an example
568	of a \KWD{throw} expression in Fortress.
569	\note{How can we tell this from the example?
570	Indeed, in general, we can't distinguish constructors from other functions
571	looking only at the call sites.}

692	dimensions. For example, the following function declares that its
693	parameter is a tuple represented in the units \EXP{\mathrm{kg}} and
694	\EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}},
695	respectively:
696	
697	\note{I MANUALLY EDITED THIS CODE -Victor}
698	%kineticEnergy(m:RR64 kg_, v:RR64 m_/s_):RR64 kg_ m_^2/s_^2 = (m v^2) / 2
699	\begin{Fortress}
700	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(m\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}, v\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}^{2} = (m\ v^{2}) / 2\)
701	\end{Fortress}
702	
703	A value of type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}} is a
704	64-bit float representing a measurement in kilograms.
705	When the function \VAR{kineticEnergy} is called, two values in its tuple
706	argument are statically checked to ensure that they are in the right units.
707	
708	All commonly used dimensions and units are provided in \library.
709	Unit symbols are encoded with trailing underscores;
710	such identifiers are rendered in roman font.
711	For example the unit \EXP{\mathrm{m}} is represented as \verb$m_$.
712	For each unit, both longhand and shorthand names are provided
713	(e.g., \EXP{\mathrm{m}},
714	\EXP{\mathrm{meter}}, and \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}).
715	The various names of a given unit can be used interchangeably.
716	Also, some units (and dimensions) are defined to be synonymous
717	with algebraic combinations of other units (and dimensions).
718	For example, the unit \EXP{\mathrm{N}} is defined to be synonymous
719	with the unit \EXP{\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}}
720	and the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Force}} is defined to be synonymous with
721	\EXP{\mathrm{Mass}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{Acceleration}}.
722	Likewise, the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Acceleration}}
723	is defined to be synonymous with \EXP{\mathrm{Velocity}/\mathrm{Time}}.
724	
725	Measurements in the same unit can be compared, added, subtracted,
726	multiplied and divided.
727	Measurements in different units can be multiplied and divided.
728	For example, we can write the following variable declaration:
729	
730	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5 seconds_
731	\begin{Fortress}
732	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
733	\end{Fortress}
734	
735	However, the following variable declaration is a static error:
736	
737	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 seconds_) / 5 seconds_
738	%I CREATED THE CODE BELOW MANUALLY -Victor
739	\begin{Fortress}
740	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{seconds}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
741	\end{Fortress}
742	
743	In addition, the following variable declaration is a static error
744	because the unit of the left hand side of this declaration
745	is \EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}}
746	whereas the unit of the right hand side
747	is simply \EXP{\mathrm{m}} (or \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}):
748	
749	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5
750	\begin{Fortress}
751	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\)
752	\end{Fortress}
753	
754	It is also possible to convert a measurement in one unit to
755	a measurement of another unit of the same dimension,
756	as in the following example:
757	
758	%kineticEnergy(3.14 kg_, 32 f_/s_ in m_/s_)
759	\begin{Fortress}
760	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(3.14\,\mathrm{kg}, 32\,\mathrm{f}/\mathrm{s} \KWD{in} \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\)
761	\end{Fortress}
762	
763	The second argument to \EXP{\VAR{kineticEnergy} } is a measurement in
764	feet per second,
765	converted to meters per second.

829	\section{Comprehensions}
830	Another way in which Fortress mimics mathematical notation is in its support for
831	\emph{comprehensions}.  Comprehensions describe the elements of a collection by
832	providing a rule that holds for all of the collection's elements.  The elements
833	of the collection are computed in parallel by default.
834	For example, we define a set \VAR{s} that consists of all elements of another
835	set \VAR{t} divided by 2, as follows:
836	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.s.tex}
837	
838	The expression to the left of the vertical bar
839	explains that elements of \VAR{s} consist of every value \EXP{x/2}
840	for every valid value of \VAR{x} (determined by the right hand side).
841	The expression to the right of the vertical bar
842	explains how the elements \VAR{x} are to be \emph{generated}
843	(in this case, from the set \VAR{t}).
844	The right hand side of a comprehension can consist of multiple generators.
845	For example, the following set consists of every element
846	resulting from the sum of an element of \VAR{s} with an element of \VAR{t}:
847	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.sum.tex}
848	
849	The right hand side of a comprehension can also contain
850	\emph{filtering expressions} to constrain the elements provided by other clauses.
851	For example, we can stipulate that \VAR{v} consists of
852	all nonnegative elements of \VAR{t} as follows:
853	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.filter.tex}
854	
855	There is a comprehension expression for every form of aggregate expression.
856	For example, here is a list comprehension in Fortress:
857	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.l.tex}
858	The elements of this list consist of
859	all elements of the set \VAR{v} multiplied by \EXP{2}.
860	
861	In the case of an array comprehension, the expression to the left of the bar
862	includes a tuple indexing the elements of the array.
863	For example, the following comprehension describes a \EXP{3 \times 3}
864	array, all of whose elements are zero.
865	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- {0,1,2}, y <- {0,1,2}]
866	\begin{Fortress}
867	\([(x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}, y \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}]\)
868	\end{Fortress}
869	
870	The collection of elements \EXP{0} through \EXP{2} can also be expressed via a range expression, as follows:
871	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- 0:2, y <- 0:2]
872	\begin{Fortress}
873	\([(x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2, y \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2]\)
874	\end{Fortress}

881	% (x,x) = 1 | x <- 0:2]
882	\begin{Fortress}

884	\( (x,x) = 1 \mid x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2]\)\-\\\poptabs
885	\end{Fortress}

890	As with mathematical notation, Fortress provides syntactic support for
891	summations and productions (and other big operations) over the elements of a collection.
892	For example, an alternative definition of \VAR{factorial} is as follows:
893	
894	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.big.tex}
895	
896	This function definition can be written in ASCII as follows:
897	
898	\begin{verbatim}
899	factorial(n) = PROD[i <- 1:n] i
900	\end{verbatim}
901	
902	The character \EXP{\prod} is written \txt{PROD}.  Likewise,

904	As with comprehensions, the values in the iteration are generated from specified collections.

906	\label{overviewTest}
907	\section{Tests and Properties}
908	Fortress includes support for automated program testing.
909	A new test in a component can be defined using the \KWD{test} modifier
910	on a top-level function definition with type ``\EXP{()\rightarrow()}''.
911	For example, here is a test function that calls the \VAR{factorial}
912	function on some representative values
913	and checks that the calls result in values greater than or equal to what was provided:
914	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Tests.tex}
915	
916	%test factorialResultLarger [x <- 0:100] = x <= factorial(x)
917	\begin{Fortress}
918	\(\KWD{test} \VAR{factorialResultLarger} [x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}100] = x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x)\)
919	\end{Fortress}
920	
921	The values for \VAR{x} are generated from the provided range
922	\EXP{0\COLONOP{}100}.
923	
924	Programs are also allowed to include \emph{property} declarations, documenting boolean conditions that a program is
925	expected to obey. Property declarations are similar syntactically to test declarations. Unlike test declarations,
926	property declarations do not specify explicit finite collections over which the property is expected to hold.
927	Instead, the parameters in a property declaration are declared to have types, and the property is expected to hold
928	over all values of those types. For example, here is a property declaring that \VAR{factorial} is greater than or equal
929	to every argument of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}:
930	
931	%property factorialResultAlwaysLarger = FORALL (x : ZZ) (x <= factorial(x))
932	\begin{Fortress}
933	\(\KWD{property} \VAR{factorialResultAlwaysLarger} = \forall (x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\; (x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x))\)
934	\end{Fortress}
935	
936	When a property declaration includes a name, the property identifier is bound to a function whose parameter and body are that of the property,
937	and whose return type is \TYP{Boolean}.
938	A function bound in this manner is referred to as a \emph{property function}.
939	A property function can be called from within tests to ensure that a
940	property holds at least for all values in some finite set of values.

942	\section{Objects and Traits}
943	\seclabel{overview-objects-traits}
944	
945	A great deal of programming can be done simply through the use of
946	functions, top-level
947	variables, and standard types. However, Fortress also includes a trait and object system for
948	defining new types, as well as objects that belong to them. Traits in Fortress exist in
949	a multiple inheritance hierarchy rooted at the traits \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.
950	\revision{revival-index}{The Working Draft of February 2011 rooted the
951	hierarchy at \TYP{Object}; \TYP{Index}, which the revival adds to the
952	library, extends only \TYP{Any} (\secref{trait-decls}).}
953	A trait declaration includes a set of method declarations,
954	some of which may be abstract.
955	For example, here is a declaration of a simple trait named \TYP{Moving}:
956

960	The set of traits extended by trait \TYP{Moving} are listed in braces after
961	\KWD{extends}. Trait \TYP{Moving} inherits all
962	methods declared by each trait it extends.
963	The two methods \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity} declared in trait \TYP{Moving}
964	are \emph{abstract}; they contain no body.
965	Their return types are vectors of length 3, whose elements are
966	of type \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
967	As in mathematical notation,
968	a vector of length $n$ with element type $T$ is written
969	\EXP{T^{n}}.
970	
971	Traits can also declare concrete methods,
972	as in the following example:
973	
974	\label{fastDim}

982	Trait declarations can be extended by other trait declarations,
983	as well as by \emph{object declarations}.
984	There are two kinds of object declarations:
985	\emph{singleton declarations} and
986	\emph{constructor declarations}.
987	
988	A singleton declaration declares a sole, stand-alone, \emph{singleton object}.
989	For example:
990	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Sol.tex}
991	
992	The object \TYP{Sol} extends two traits: \TYP{Moving} and \TYP{Stellar},
993	and provides definitions for the abstract methods it inherits. Objects must
994	provide concrete definitions for all abstract methods they inherit. \TYP{Sol}
995	also defines a field \VAR{spectralClass}.
996	For every field included in an object
997	definition, an implicit getter is defined for that field. Calls to
998	the getter of the field of an object consist of an expression
999	denoting the object
1000	followed by a dot and the name of the field. For example, here is a call to the
1001	getter \VAR{spectralClass} of object \TYP{Sol}:
1002	
1003	
1004	
1005	%Sol.spectralClass
1006	\begin{Fortress}
1007	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass}\)
1008	\end{Fortress}
1009	
1010	If a field includes modifier \KWD{settable},
1011	an implicit setter is defined for the
1012	field. Calls to setters look like assignments.
1013	Here is an assignment to field \VAR{spectralClass}
1014	of object \TYP{Sol}:
1015	
1016	%Sol.spectralClass := G3
1017	\begin{Fortress}
1018	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass} \ASSIGN G_{3}\)
1019	\end{Fortress}
1020	
1021	In fact,
1022	all accesses to a field from outside the object to which the field belongs
1023	must go through the getter of the field, and all assignments to it must go
1024	through the setter. (There is simply no other way
1025	syntactically to refer to the field.)
1026	
1027	If a field includes modifier \KWD{hidden}, no implicit getter is defined for the object.
1028	
1029	
1030	The self parameter of a method can be given a position other than the default
1031	position. For example, here is a definition of a type where the
1032	self parameters appear in nonstandard positions:

1037	Calls to these methods look more like function calls than method calls. For example, in the following
1038	call to \VAR{append}, the receiver of the call is \EXP{l_{2}}:
1039	
1040	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.append.tex}

1042	
1043	A constructor declaration declares an \emph{object constructor}.
1044	In contrast to singleton declarations, a constructor declaration includes
1045	value parameters in its header, as in the following example:
1046	\label{particleDim}
1047	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Particle.tex}

1050	For example:
1051	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.p1.tex}

1054	fields of the object, along with their getters (by default). These parameters

1059	In the definition of \TYP{Particle}, it is the implicitly defined getters of

1063	In both singleton and constructor declarations,
1064	implicitly defined getters and setters can be overridden by defining
1065	explicit getters and setters,
1066	using the modifiers \KWD{getter} and \KWD{setter}. For example,
1067	we alter the definition
1068	of \TYP{Particle} to include an explicit
1069	getter for field \VAR{velocity} as follows:

1071	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1072	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)

1074	%  getter velocity() = do
1075	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1076	%    velocity
1077	%  end
1078	%end
1079	\begin{Fortress}
1080	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\

1082	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1083	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1084	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\

1086	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1087	\(\KWD{end}\)
1088	\end{Fortress}

1090	The explicitly defined getter first prints a message and then returns
1091	the value of the
1092	field \VAR{velocity}. \emph{Note that the final variable reference in this getter refers
1093	directly to the field \VAR{velocity}, not to the getter.} Only within an object definition

1095	accessed directly when they are referred to as simple variables. In the following definition
1096	of \TYP{Particle}, the getter \VAR{velocity} is recursively accessed through the special variable

1098	
1099	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1100	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)
1101	%  extends Moving
1102	%  getter velocity() = do
1103	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1104	%    self.velocity
1105	%  end
1106	%end
1107	\begin{Fortress}
1108	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\
1109	\(                \VAR{velocity} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3})\)\-\\\poptabs
1110	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1111	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1112	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\
1113	\(    \mathord{\KWD{self}}.\VAR{velocity}\)\-\\\poptabs
1114	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1115	\(\KWD{end}\)
1116	\end{Fortress}
1117	
1118	Now, the result of a call to getter \VAR{velocity} is an infinite loop (along with a lot of output).

1120	\subsection{Traits, Getters, and Setters}
1121	Although traits do not include field declarations, they can include getter and setter declarations, as in the following
1122	alternative definition of trait \TYP{Moving}:
1123	
1124	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1125	%  getter position(): (RR Length)^3
1126	%  getter velocity(): (RR Velocity)^3
1127	%end
1128	\begin{Fortress}
1129	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1130	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{position}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1131	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1132	\(\KWD{end}\)
1133	\end{Fortress}
1134	
1135	Now, an object extending trait \TYP{Moving} must provide the definitions of
1136	\emph{getters} (as opposed to ordinary methods)
1137	for \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity}.
1138	The advantage of this definition is that we can use getter
1139	notation on a variable of static type \TYP{Moving}:
1140	
1141	% v : Moving = ...
1142	% v.position
1143	\begin{Fortress}
1144	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Moving} = \ldots\)\\
1145	\( v.\VAR{position}\)\-\\\poptabs
1146	\end{Fortress}
1147	
1148	In fact, getters can be declared in a trait definition using field declaration syntax, as in the following example
1149	(which is equivalent to the definition of \TYP{Moving} above):
1150	
1151	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1152	%  position: (RR Length)^3
1153	%  velocity: (RR Velocity)^3
1154	%end
1155	\begin{Fortress}
1156	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1157	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{position}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1158	\(  \VAR{velocity}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1159	\(\KWD{end}\)
1160	\end{Fortress}
1161	
1162	Getter declarations in trait definitions must not include bodies.
1163	A getter declaration can include the various modifiers
1164	allowed on a field declaration, with similar results.
1165	For example, if the modifier \KWD{settable} is used, then a
1166	setter is implicitly declared, in addition to a getter.

1168	\section{Features for Library Development}
1169	The language features introduced above are sufficient for the vast majority of applications programming. However, Fortress
1170	has also designed to be a good language for \emph{library} programming. In fact, much of the Fortress language as viewed
1171	by applications programmers actually consists of code defined in libraries, written in a small core language. By defining as
1172	much of the language as possible in libraries, our aim is to allow the language to evolve gracefully as new demands are placed on it.
1173	In this section, we briefly mention some of the features that make Fortress a good language for library development.
1174	
1175	\subsection{Generic Types and Static Parameters}
1176	As in other languages, Fortress allows types to be parametric with respect to other types, as well as other ``static'' parameters,
1177	including integers, booleans, dimensions, units, and operators.
1178	Fortress provides some standard parametric types,
1179	such as \TYP{Array} and \TYP{Vector}.
1180	Programmers can also define new traits, objects, and functions that include static parameters.
1181	
1182	\subsection{Specification of Locality and Data Distribution}
1183	Fortress includes a facility for expressing programmer intent concerning the distribution of large data structures
1184	at run time. This intent is expressed through special data structures called \emph{distributions}.
1185	In fact, all arrays and matrices include distributions. These distributions
1186	are defined in \library.
1187	In most cases, the default distributions
1188	will provide programmers with good performance over a variety of machines. However, in some circumstances,
1189	performance can be improved by overriding the default selection of distributions.
1190	Moreover, some programmers might wish to define new distributions, tailored for particular
1191	platforms and programs.
1192	
1193	\subsection{Operator Overloading}
1194	Operators in Fortress can be overloaded with new definitions.
1195	Here is an alternative definition of the \VAR{factorial} function, defined as a postfix operator:
1196	
1197	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.factorial.tex}
1198	
1199	As with mathematical notation, Fortress allows operators to be defined as prefix, postfix,
1200	and infix. More exotic operators can even be defined as subscripting (i.e., applications of the
1201	operators look like subscripts), and as bracketing (i.e., applications of the operators
1202	look like the operands have been simply enclosed in brackets).
1203	
1204	\subsection{Definition of New Syntax}
1205	Fortress provides a facility for the definition of new syntax in libraries.
1206	This facility is useful for defining libraries for domain-specific languages,
1207	such
1208	as SQL, XML, etc.
1209	It is also used to encode some of
1210	the language constructs seen by applications
1211	programmers.
1212

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
52

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	## The library order
74	
75	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76	
77	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78	
79	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81	
82	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
86	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
87	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
90	
91	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
92	
93	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
94	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
95	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
96	
97	## Name resolution
98	
99	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
100	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
101	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
102	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
103	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
104	
105	## Building
106	
107	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
108	
109	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
110	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
111	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
113	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
114	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
115	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
116	
117	## After an edit of the library
118	
119	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
120	
121	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
122	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
123	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
124	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
125	
126	## Symptoms of a skipped step
127	
128	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
129	
130	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
131	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
132	
133	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
134	
135	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
136	
137	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
138	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
139	
140	Two more facts help you read a run:
141	
142	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
143	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
144

\subsection{The programming environment of the overview}
\seclabel{revival-environment}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{programming-env}, \secref{overview:apis} and
\secref{apitool}; the head of \chapref{components}.
\item[Change] The three sections are rewritten as a guide to the
implementation in the revival's repository: the Java version and the build; a
program run under the interpreter; the compilation of the compiled path's
library, and the same program compiled and run; an API and two components,
run under the interpreter, then linked and run; an API generated from a
component.
Each command was issued as printed in a new checkout of the repository, and
each output is printed as that run gave it.
The text names the caches of the implementation where the Working Draft spoke
of a fortress, says ``file extension'' where the Working Draft said
``suffix'', and states once for a component and once for an API that a file
holds exactly one, whose name is the file's name without its file extension,
with the message that the implementation prints when the names differ.
The function \VAR{run} takes no parameter in any example or sentence.
The commands \txt{remove}, \txt{removeApi}, \txt{upgrade} and \txt{upgradeAll}
are not in the chapter.
One box at the head of \secref{programming-env} covers the three sections.
Two draft notes at the head of the chapter are taken out with the text that
they spoke of: the sentence ``From \secref{programming-env} to
\secref{apitool} are out of date.'' and the note on the removal of APIs from
fortresses, both quoted below.
The text of \chapref{components} is unchanged; a box at its head says which of
its operations the implementation has.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
decision of 16~November 2026, of the curator of the revival, that the
revival's edition of this specification describes the implementation as it is,
so that a reader who follows \chapref{overview} can use the repository.
The Working Draft's text of these sections is a splice of two editions that
the team made on 5~November 2009 and marked ``out of date'' in the same
commit.
It describes a \emph{fortress}, a persistent store of compiled components that
performs the operations on them, which the team did not build, and it gives
commands that the implementation does not have or that mean another thing
there: \txt{fortress run} on a source file, \txt{fortress} as an abbreviation
of \txt{fortress run}, \txt{fortress remove}, \txt{fortress removeApi},
\txt{fortress upgrade} and \txt{fortress upgradeAll}.
Its sentences on \VAR{run} speak of a parameter \VAR{args} that the team took
out of the API \TYP{Executable} on 13~March 2009; its examples
\txt{HelloWorld3.fss} and \txt{HelloWorld4.fss} still declare it.
It says that a source file must contain exactly one component declaration, and
in the next sentence that a compiled file may include several.
The splice also lost a command.
The text speaks of a compound component \TYP{Gary} that no command of it
makes.
Version 1.0$\beta$ of the specification (6~March 2007, section 2.2) printed
the command, after the two commands that compile \txt{Ralph.fss} and
\txt{Blargh.fss}:
\begin{quote}
\txt{fortress link Gary from Ralph with Blargh}

The first two commands compile files \txt{Ralph.fss} and \txt{Blargh.fss},
respectively, and install them in the resident fortress.
The third command tells the resident fortress to link components \TYP{Ralph}
and \TYP{Blargh} together into a compound component, named \TYP{Gary}.
\TYP{Gary} is an executable component; we can execute it directly with the
command:

\txt{fortress run Gary}
\end{quote}
With that command in the place of the Working Draft's third command,
\txt{fortress run Blargh.fss}, and of the paragraph after it, the original
text below reads whole.
The design of fortresses with the operations upgrade, extract and install is

# The specification as HTML for a phone

`spec2html.py` converts the specification's LaTeX into a reader of static pages: the front matter, the 43 chapters and the 10 appendices, 54 pages. GitHub Pages serves them once `main` is pushed (`.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `docs/`). Nothing comes from another site.

## The two editions

The curator's decision of 2026-11-15: the team's text has the public address, and the revival's edition steps back, out of the search engines. `--source` names the source root, and the source root names the edition.

| | The Working Draft of 2 February 2011 | The revised edition of the 2026 revival |
|---|---|---|
| `--source` | `Specification-1.0-frozen` | `Specification` (the default) |
| Pages | `docs/specification/`, https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/ | `docs/specification/revival/` |
| Beside the LaTeX, the conversion reads | the team's tree at the draft's commit `2f8b4331a` (F-163): `SpecData/`, `Fortify/`, the `.fsi` files of the library, taken from git into the work folder | the working tree |
| Work folder | `/tmp/spec-html-work-draft` | `/tmp/spec-html-work` |
| The revival's layer (callouts, tint, legend, "archived copy" links) | none | as before |
| `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` | on no page | on every page |
| What the edition adds, and where | the reader's controls; the lines that start "This edition:" in small monospace (class `edline`): one under the title of the contents, one over each library listing, one in the front matter, and the foot of each page | one line at the top of each page (class `edline top`): "The Fortress revival's revised edition of 2026, not the text of the Fortress team", with a link to the same page of the Working Draft |
| Storage in the browser | `fortress-spec.*`, the keys in use since the first sample | `fortress-spec-revival.*` |

- **The pointer at the foot of a Working Draft page** links to the same chapter of the revised edition and says one of three things. "Changed this chapter": the chapter's LaTeX differs under the two roots (the chapter's own text and every file that it reads, comments apart; `chapter_latex`); 28 pages. "Did not change the text of this chapter; … its examples or library listings are those of the tree of 2026": the LaTeX is the same, and an example, a table of reserved words or a listed `.fsi` file differs (`chapter_companions`); 2 pages, the two chapters of library listings. "Did not change this chapter": 24 pages.
- **`editions.html`**, written by the build of the Working Draft and linked from the contents page of both editions, lists 1.0α, 1.0β, 1.0, the Working Draft and, set apart under "Not the team's work", the revised edition. Its dates and facts are from `Specification-history/README.md`, `explorations/coordinator/spec-editions-leads-2026-11-10.md`, F-163, `pdfinfo` and git. The build copies the three PDFs into `docs/specification/pdf/` (2.4, 2.0 and 1.2 MB; the same blobs as in the tree, so the repository does not grow). The PDF of the revised edition (2.5 MB) is linked at its GitHub address, not served from the site. The tree holds no PDF build of the Working Draft of 2011.
- **`revised-only.js`**, written by the build of the Working Draft from the pages of the revised edition: for each chapter, the ids of the blocks that only the revised edition has. Both editions load it (see "The notes across the two editions").
- **Build order.** The revised edition first, then the Working Draft, which reads the revised pages for `revised-only.js`. A crawler's `robots.txt` cannot be served for this site from this repository (it is read at the host's root only), so the `noindex` tag is the measure; `check.js` checks it on every page of both editions.
- **The examples of the Working Draft** are set as the team's tree of February 2011 set them: its `foreg` writes the `Fortress` environment, where the later tree's writes `FortressCode`. The converter takes both.

A first sample of 2026-11-10 held the front matter and chapters 1 to 6. The curator read it and decided how the rest is made; `curator-notes.md` holds his words. This run follows them:

1. Examples and displays are LaTeX converted to SVG. The converter's own rendering of displayed code and formulas is gone.
2. Code words and formulas inside a sentence stay HTML text, with the three rules of `reader.css` that he approved (no ligatures in code, the inline highlight with narrow side padding, serif curly quotation marks). Those rules are unchanged.
3. Every table and display is compared with the PDF. "The checks" below says how, and what a person still has to look at.
4. An address of the authors' text gets the edition's link to the Internet Archive.
5. The revival's paragraph in the preface has the tint of the revival's additions, and the opening explains the tint.
6. A quote pair around the whole of a typewriter span is curly; an apostrophe inside code stays as typed.
7. Where the specification shows ASCII, the page shows ASCII.

## The files

- `spec2html.py`: the conversion and the site's pages. Python 3 with its standard library and `fontTools` (to read the fonts it makes). It runs `latex`, `dvisvgm` and Emacs (for the tree's Fortify).
- `reader.css`, `reader.js`: the reader. The build copies them into `docs/specification/`.
- `check.js`: the reader in Chromium at a phone's width (below).
- `compare.js`: every display in Chromium against LaTeX's own picture of it (below).
- `pdfcheck.py`: the words of every block against the words of a PDF (below).
- `notes-export-2026-11-15.txt`: the curator's 15 notes as he exported them before the editions were parted; `check.js` imports them.
- `curator-notes.md`: the curator's decisions and notes.
- `widthless-glyphs-2026-11-16.md`: every place of a glyph of no width in the displays of both editions, by page and section (see "The glyphs of no width").

The build also writes `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/` in each edition's folder: the fonts of the displays.

## Running it

From the repository root:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --list            # every chapter with its slug
    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try variables,functions
    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try all
    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py                   # the revised edition, into docs/specification/revival/
    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --source Specification-1.0-frozen   # the Working Draft, into docs/specification/

`--source` goes with every form above (`--list`, `--try`).

- A plain run takes about a minute when the work folder is warm, and about three minutes when it is empty. It rewrites every page of its edition's folder: the 54 chapter pages, `index.html` (the contents), `notes.html`, `references.html`, `reader.css`, `reader.js`, `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/`. No page is edited by hand.
- `--try` converts into the work folder only (`<work>/try/`, with the reader's files, so the pages can be opened) and prints, for each chapter, what did not convert. It writes nothing under `docs/`.
- `--chapters a,b` publishes only those chapters; a cross-reference into a chapter that is left out shows its number and "[not converted yet]".
- The script exits 1 if a published chapter holds a construct that it did not convert, a display on which LaTeX reported an error, or a display that uses a character that the fonts lack. Such a place shows in the page in red, and the report names it.
- `--work` sets the scratch folder (by default one for each edition, see the table): the examples as Fortify renders them, the LaTeX file of each chapter's displays with its log, the SVGs, the fonts. `--base` sets the public address that the links of exported notes start with.
- For the revised edition the script reads `Specification/`, `SpecData/examples/`, `SpecData/tables/`, `Fortify/`, and the `.fsi` files of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`; for the Working Draft it reads `Specification-1.0-frozen/` and the same folders as `git archive 2f8b4331a` gives them. It writes nothing in the original tree. It builds and runs no Fortress.

## How the text is converted

The script is a converter of its own over the macros that the chapters use (`pandoc` and `htlatex` were tried on the first sample: the first drops Fortify's markup without a word, the second stops under the tree's macros).

- **Structure.** It walks the `\input`s from `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` and numbers parts, chapters, sections, subsections, figures, lemmas and theorems as LaTeX does. Each page is one chapter. A section's anchor is its label (`\seclabel{overview:apis}` gives `#sec-overview-apis`); a section without a label gets `#s-` and its title.
- **Running text** becomes HTML: paragraphs, lists, headings, footnotes, the authors' `\note` boxes ("Draft note"), the revival's `\revision` callouts. Fortify's markup and formulas inside a sentence become HTML text with Unicode characters, italics, superscripts and subscripts. The `\newcommand`s of `Specification/latex-common/macros/` are read and expanded, and so are the definitions that a chapter makes for itself (`\def`, `\newcommand`, `\renewcommand`, `\RenewDocumentCommand`), and the macro files that Appendix A reads for each of its calculi, in its order.
- **Displays** are set by LaTeX. A display is an example (`\begin{Fortress}`, or a file of `SpecData/examples/` that the tree's tool `foreg` renders, as the specification's `ant genSource` does), a displayed formula (`\[ \]`, `$$ $$`, `align`, `eqnarray`), a table (`tabular`, `array`), a grammar box (`Grammar`, `GrammarTwo`), a `tabbing` or `ttt` block, a drawing (`*.eepic`), and a table of reserved words (written as the build's Perl scripts write it). For each chapter the script writes one LaTeX file with the preamble of `fortress.tex` and one page for each display, in a box of the PDF's text width; the chapter's own definitions go into the file at their places; the labels of the whole specification go into its `.aux` file, so that a reference inside a display prints its number and links to its page. `latex` sets the file, `dvisvgm` converts each page, and the script puts the SVG into the page, inline.
  - The text of a display is SVG text in the TeX fonts, so it can be selected and copied. The fonts are made by dvisvgm from the fonts of the TeX installation and are served from `fonts/`; a page loads only those that it shows.
  - One SVG serves the light and the dark theme: its ink is `currentColor`, the colour of the text around it.
  - A display wider than the screen scrolls sideways inside its frame, at the PDF's proportions: a display is not reflowed.
  - A footnote inside a display joins the chapter's footnotes, and the display shows its number.
